newsitem.title: POLAND: NEW POLISH FINMIN BELKA VOWS POLICY CONTINUITY.
newsitem.headline: NEW POLISH FINMIN BELKA VOWS POLICY CONTINUITY.

text.p: Poland's new Finance Minister Marek Belka, due to replace Grzegorz Kolodko on Tuesday, said he wanted to continue a policy of macroeconomic consolidation, curbing inflation and controlling the budget gap.
Belka, 45, told Reuters in a telephone interview he also wanted to speed up implementation of major structural reforms such as the privatisation of banks and social security reform.

"My policy will be that of full and active continuation of a policy of macroeconomic consolidation, fighting inflation and controlling the budget," said Belka, an independent economist currently advising President Aleksander Kwasniewski.

"I would like to participate more actively in the speeding up of several structural reforms awaiting us," he said adding he would pay special attention to bank privatisaton and the long-delayed overhaul of the creaking social security system.

Belka said he would not seek to cut inflation at all costs because such a policy would bring economic collapse, but that curbing price growth was a necessary condition for sustaining Poland's economic growth.
"We could cut inflation down to one digit in a short time, but that would be at the cost of economic collapse," he said.

"But fast economic growth cannot be sustained with inflation at current levels -- it has to be reduced for the growth to be permanent," Belka said. "Without single digit inflation, for instance, we can only talk about an increase in housing output," he added.
Poland's year-on-year inflation in 1996 fell to 18.5 percent from 21.6 percent in 1995 and the budget draft for this year sees its further fall to 13 percent in December 1997.
Polish gross domestic product (GDP) rose six percent last year after a seven percent growth in 1995 and is forecast by the government to rise 5.5 percent this year.
Belka said that although he did not participate in drafting the 1997 budget law, he fully supported the goals it set.
"Everything has to be done to reach the (inflation, GDP growth) goals envisaged by the budget," he said.

Belka is an economics professor at the Polish Academy of Sciences specialising in banking and monetary policies. He is an author of studies on Milton Friedman and the economic policies of the U.S. Ronald Reagan administration.
He was a World Bank and International Finance Corporation (IFC) consultant from 1991 to 1993 and also a finance ministry consultant from 1992 to 1993.
He became the presidential economic adviser after ex-communist Aleksander Kwasniewski beat incumbent Lech Walesa in 1995 presidential polls.

Leszek Balcerowicz, the leader of the opposition Union for Freedom and the architect of Poland's market reforms started in 1989, praised Belka's knowledge but said was untested in the policy hot seat.

"I know Professor Marek Belka as very a good economist who knows western economy well, but I cannot say anything about his ability to make decisions in difficult matters such as economic policy," Balcerowicz told the private Radio Zet.
Western diplomats said that although they were sorry to see Kolodko go, Belka's appointment was not a cause for concern.

"Mr Belka has very sound views, convictions and with such background he is extremely suited (for the post), although he can be tested only on the job," a senior representative of an international financial institution said.
"He is a straight continuation of what has made Poland do well over the past seven years, which is a basic consensus on sound finance and market-oriented structural reforms," he said.
